per_ply.system_comment: The most accurate move is dxc5, which holds the balance (+0.22, Stockfish:16) along [pv:dxc5 Nc6 Qb3 Ndb4 Nc3]. White immediately wins a pawn, and the line may leave Black's king under pressure—central material with initiative is hard to pass up. Na3 leads to equality along [pv:Na3 Bg4 dxc5 e6 Re1], a comparable option where Black's pawn structure could be weakened further down the line, but dxc5 is preferable for the instant pawn and clearer attacking prospects that set up sharper queenside play to come.

The most accurate move, holding the balance (+0.07, Stockfish:16) along [pv:b4 Ne6 Qb3 Nb6 Rd1]: b4 immediately leaves Black with a hanging piece and targets the knight on c5. In the line, White's pieces may grow more active and the rooks could take over the open files—rooks on open files often dictate the endgame. Re1 leads to equality along [pv:Re1 Nb6 Qc2 Nba4 Qc4], where Black's king may come under pressure, but b4 is stronger for punishing the loose piece at once.

The most accurate move, holding the balance (+0.03, Stockfish:16) along [pv:a5 Nc3 Nxc3 Bxc3 axb4]. With...a5 Black immediately opens the a-file for the rook—a file rooks can dominate once it clears. Deeper in that line Black's rooks may grow more active on the open files, though in return the pawn structure could turn weaker as structural flaws emerge. Nb6 leads to equality [pv:Nb6 Qe2 Qd5 Rd1 Qc4], a comparable option that immediately targets the queen on d1 and gains space, but...a5 is the stronger choice for activating the rook on the newly opened a-file.

per_ply.human_comment: (!) Threatens 22...Nf4 23.gxf4 Rxd2

Only nervousnes
s can explain such a mistake by Alekhine. It was necessary to defend with 23.
Rac1. Witnesses tell that right in that moment a waiter brought some coffee to
Alekhine. He thanked the waiter and still looking at the chessboard put a
piece of sugar in the coffee cup. Only at the last moment he realized that it
was not a piece of sugar but ... a white pawn. While he realized his mistake,
he got upset, said something, pushed the cup away and .... coffee spilled out
of the cup. Mikenas too noticed his opponent apparent nervousness, and perhaps
distracted by this fact he immediately took the Knight.
per_ply.system_comment: Ne4 makes matters worse, and Black now has a decisive advantage (-0.90 → -3.86, Stockfish:16) [pv:Ne4 Rc2 Qd3 Rxb2 Rac1]. White leaves a piece hanging, and Rc2 is the refutation that punishes it; deeper in the line Black may gain two pieces for a knight. White missed the chance to make Black's pieces passive and to target the queen on g4 with Nd4, which still leads to a clear advantage for Black [pv:Nd4 Qxe2 Rxe2 Bd3 Ree1].

per_ply.human_comment:
After this
move Mikenas realized that strangely his opponent was smiling. With a
trembling hand Alekhine pointed to the c2 square and said:" Young man, if you
played Rc2 you had won at once." Mikenas confesses: "Only after Alekhine's
words I realized that I had such an opportunity."
per_ply.system_comment: Bxe4 pins a White piece immediately, but Qxe4 is the refutation that punishes the exchange, and after (-3.86 → -0.60, Stockfish:16) on [pv:Bxe4 Qxe4 Qxe4 Rxe4 Rc5] Black's advantage shrinks sharply. Deeper in the line, Black may lose the bishop-pair edge that often sustains long-term pressure. Black missed the chance to keep two bishops for a knight and reach the seventh rank with Rc2, which leaves Black with a decisive advantage on [pv:Rc2 Qd3 Rxb2 Rac1 a4].

Qxe4 is White's most accurate try, leaving Black with a hanging piece and targeting the queen on g4 while setting up the possibility of opening the a-file for the rook deeper in the line, though at the cost of a pawn structure that may become weaker with doubled, isolated, and backward pawns. The position still leads to a slight advantage for Black (-0.58, Stockfish:16) on [pv:Qxe4 Qxe4 Rxe4 Rc5 a4], clearly preferable to Kg1, which leaves Black with a decisive advantage on [pv:Kg1 Bxf3 h3 Nf4 hxg4].

By taking on e4, White sets up the possibility of opening the a-file for the rook deeper in the line, making this the strongest practical try even though it leads to a slight advantage for Black (-0.62, Stockfish:16) on [pv:Rxe4 Rc5 a4 Rc2 Bd4]; in return, the continuation may leave Black with a rook on the seventh rank at c2. Open files are prime routes for rook activity. Kg2 was clearly weaker, leaving Black with a decisive advantage on [pv:Kg2 Qg4 Bc1 Rc3 Ng5]. The queens are off — the game enters its final phase, where technique matters more than tactics. The position stays balanced.

Bd4 is White's best available move, yet it still leads to a slight advantage for Black, (-0.53, Stockfish:16), on [pv:Bd4 e6 Ree1 a4 Kg2], at the cost of a continuation that may leave White's king under pressure—once king safety erodes, defense is much harder to coordinate. Rb1 is clearly weaker, leading to a clear advantage for Black on [pv:Rb1 Rxf2 Nd4 a4 Ne2], a line that could still leave Black with a hanging piece but cannot rescue White's position.

per_ply.system_comment: The strongest move, maintaining Black's advantage (-0.32, Stockfish:16) on [pv:Bf8 Kg1 Bb4 Kf2 Ra2], consolidating the bishop in this rook endgame. The line may leave White with a hanging piece, pressuring weak enemy material—loose pieces often decide these endings. b6 was a comparable option that leads to equality on [pv:b6 Kg2 Bf8 Kf3 Bc5], but Bf8 keeps the stronger continuation.

By playing Kh3, White improves the activity of the pieces—actively placed pieces tend to create more practical chances in rook endgames—but the move still leads to a slight advantage for Black (-0.52, Stockfish:16) on [pv:Kh3 Ra2 Nc1 Rxa4 Kg4]. Kf2 was a comparable option that also leads to a slight advantage for Black on [pv:Kf2 Ra2 Rc1 Rxa4 Kf3], as that line could leave White's rooks more active on the open files.

The strongest move, maintaining Black's advantage (-0.68, Stockfish:16) on [pv:Ra2 Nc1 Rxa4 Rh1 Ra3], as the line may set up a passed pawn on a5—an endgame asset that can decide the fight if it advances. Further along, active rook play on the c-file can deepen the pressure. b6 leads to a slight advantage for Black on [pv:b6 Kg4 Ra2 Nc1 Rxa4], a roughly comparable option.

43.Rc1 is the strongest move here, leads to a clear advantage for Black: [pv:Rc1 Rxe2 Rc8+ Ke7 Rxe2] (-0.97, Stockfish:16). This sets up the following deeper in the line: Black has a hanging piece and White has a rook on the seventh rank (c7). A comparable alternative was Nc1, which leads to a clear advantage for Black after [pv:Nc1 Bxe1 Nxa2 Bd2 Rc4]. Black's pieces become more passive.

Ke7 is the most accurate move, maintaining Black's advantage (-0.73, Stockfish:16) on [pv:Ke7 Rc7+ Kf8 Rxe2 Rxe2] as the king centralizes before weathering White's rook activity on the c-file. Kd7 would instead hand White a clear advantage on [pv:Kd7 Rec4 Bd6 exd6 f5+], where Black immediately leaves a piece hanging and targets the rook on c8—a shaky route when Ke7 keeps the king ready for the forcing f5+ check that follows.

Black's 45...f5+ maintains the advantage (-1.09, Stockfish:16) on [pv:f5+ exf6+ Kxf6 R4c7 e5], opening with a forcing check that pulls the king to f6 and is set to continue with...R4c7 and...e5 deeper in the line. Red2 was a comparable option that also leads to a clear advantage for Black on [pv:Red2 R4c7+ Rd7 b6 Rxc7], where Black has won a piece for a pawn and the rooks are active on the open files—coordination on open files often decides endgames—while f5+ keeps White tied down from the first move.

The most accurate choice maintains Black's advantage (-1.08, Stockfish:16) on [pv:Kxf6 R4c7 e5 Rxb7 exf4], confirming Black's bishop-for-pawn win—a material edge that weighs heavily in the endgame. The continuation may weaken White's pawn structure further and activate Black's rooks on open files, though in return Black risks leaving a piece hanging. By contrast, Kf7 leads to a clear advantage for White on [pv:Kf7 Kg5 Bd6 Rd8 Rg2], which is why Kxf6 is clearly preferable.

With R4c7, White may set up targeting Black's rook on e6 in the line [pv:R4c7 e5 Rxb7 exf4 Rc6+], where Black's e5 could open the e-file for the rook—a file that often decides endgames—yet the move still leads to a clear advantage for Black (-1.05, Stockfish:16). Rh8 was clearly weaker by comparison, giving Black a winning advantage on [pv:Rh8 Rh2 Rxh2 Rxh2 Rc7].

per_ply.system_comment: White's Kf3 leads to a clear advantage for Black (-1.28, Stockfish:16) on [pv:Kf3 Rgf2+ Ke4 Rae2+ Kd5], as the king walk gains nothing while the continuation may leave Black's rooks more active on the open files—active rooks on open files are a lasting endgame edge. Rae2+ is Black's strongest continuation, maintaining the advantage (-1.34, Stockfish:16) by taking immediate control of the center on [pv:Rae2+ Kd4 Re6 Rc6 Rxf4+]; with the white king driven, the line may set up pressure against the rook on c6 and could consolidate Black's bishop-for-pawn edge. Central control here keeps Black's pieces coordinated as the endgame unfolds. Rfe2+ is a roughly comparable alternative that leads to a clear advantage for Black on [pv:Rfe2+ Kf3 Rf2+ Ke4 Rae2+].

White's Kd3 leads to a clear advantage for Black (-1.28, Stockfish:16) after [pv:Kd3 Re1 Rc6+ Kf5 Rf7+], as Black's Re1 and the checks on c6 and f7 drive the white king forward without respite. Kd4 was a comparable option that also leads to a clear advantage for Black on [pv:Kd4 Re6 Rc6 Rxf4+ Kd3], where White may pin a black piece and could target the rook on e6 deeper in the line, though Kd3 keeps the king slightly better placed while still falling short.

Black's most accurate move maintains the advantage (-1.34, Stockfish:16) on [pv:Re6 Rc6 Rf3+ Kc4 Rxf4+], accepting that in the line White's king may reach safety—in endgames, a sheltered king can shore up defense, but Black still keeps the better position. Re1 is roughly as good, also leading to a clear advantage for Black on [pv:Re1 Rc6+ Kf5 Rf7+ Kg4].

White's Rc6 leads to a clear advantage for Black (-1.34, Stockfish:16) after [pv:Rc6 Rf3+ Kd4 Rxf4+ Kd3], as the check on f3 drives the king forward and Black soon takes on f4 with Rxf4+. Rc1 is a roughly comparable option that still gives Black a winning advantage on [pv:Rc1 Rd2+ Kc4 Ba3 Rb1], where White's rook may get behind the passed pawn in the line—a typical way to support its advance in rook endings.

Black's most accurate move, maintaining Black's advantage (-1.34, Stockfish:16) on [pv:Rf3+ Kc4 Rxf4+ Kb3 Rxc6], as the check may lead to a safer king while the line could leave White's pawn structure weaker — damaged pawn formations are hard to hold in rook endings. Rd2+ is a comparable option that leads to a clear advantage for Black on [pv:Rd2+ Kc4 Rc2+ Kd5 Rcxc6], though it is set to leave White's pieces more passive rather than press the pawn weaknesses as directly.

Walking the king to d4 leads to a clear advantage for Black (-1.31, Stockfish:16), and after [pv:Kd4 Rxf4+ Kd3 Rxc6 bxc6] Black's pieces are actively placed — in endgames, active pieces often translate into lasting pressure. Kc4 is a comparable option that also leads to a clear advantage for Black [pv:Kc4 Rc3+ Kd5 Rcxc6 bxc6], though deeper in that line White's passed pawn may advance dangerously far forward.

Black's Rxf4+ maintains the advantage (-1.31, Stockfish:16) on [pv:Rxf4+ Kd5 Rf5+ Kd4 Rxc6], though in return Black leaves a piece hanging. After Kd5, Rf5+ is the accurate follow-up in this line. Rxc6 is a comparable option that also leads to a clear advantage for Black [pv:Rxc6 bxc6 Rxf4+ Kd3 Ke6], leaving White's pieces passive right away and offering a line where Black may win a piece for a pawn.

White may target the bishop on b4 deeper in the line, but Kd5 leads to a clear advantage for Black (-1.27, Stockfish:16) after [pv:Kd5 Rf5+ Kd4 Rxc6 bxc6]. Kd3 is a comparable option that also leads to a clear advantage for Black [pv:Kd3 Rxc6 bxc6 Ke6 Rh7], where White could eventually gain an outside passed pawn—often a decisive asset in rook endings.

Black's most accurate continuation, maintaining the advantage (-1.31, Stockfish:16), as the check [pv:Rf5+ Kd4 Rxc6 bxc6 Ke6] may leave White's pieces passive deeper in the line—restricting enemy activity often decides rook endings. By contrast, Rxc6 leads to only a slight advantage for Black [pv:Rxc6 Kxc6 Rc4+ Kb6 Bc3] and could leave White with a hanging piece, but it is clearly weaker than the precise check.

Kd4 is White's strongest king move, setting up safer king placement deeper in the line—king safety matters once rooks activate on open files—but it still leads to a clear advantage for Black (-1.27, Stockfish:16) after [pv:Kd4 Rxc6 bxc6 Ke6 Rh7]. Kc4 is roughly as good, also leading to a clear advantage for Black via [pv:Kc4 Rxc6+ bxc6 Rc5+ Kb3], and immediately targets the bishop on b4.

The strongest continuation, 56...Rxc6, maintains Black's advantage (-1.30, Stockfish:16) by winning a bishop for a pawn, while the line [pv:Rxc6 bxc6 Ke6 Rh7 Kd6] may leave White with a hanging piece. Rf4+ is a comparable option that leads to a clear advantage for Black [pv:Rf4+ Kd5 Rf5+ Kd4 Rxc6], also netting a piece for a pawn with more active piece placement, though Rxc6 remains the most accurate choice.

White's 57.bxc6 pushes the dangerously advanced passed pawn forward and activates the rooks on the open files, but at the cost of giving Black a bishop for a pawn. That trade still leads to a clear advantage for Black (-1.34, Stockfish:16) in [pv:bxc6 Ke6 Rh7 Kd6 c7], yet it is stronger than the runner-up 57.b6, which would leave Black with a decisive advantage [pv:b6 Bc5+ Ke4 Rxb6 Rh7]; White's follow-up 58.Rb5 only deepens the trouble.

58.Rb5 makes matters worse — Black now has a decisive advantage (-1.29 → -31.56, Stockfish:16). 58...Rxb5 punishes the rook move, and [pv:Rb5 Rxb5 axb5 Kd6 Kd3] drives White's king back with nothing gained for the exchange; even 59.axb5 will not claw back equality. White missed the chance to keep pieces actively placed — vital when every tempo counts in the endgame — with 58.Rh7, which leads to a clear advantage for Black [pv:Rh7 Kd6 c7 Rc5 c8=Q], a far less damaging line than what occurred.

White's 59.axb5 fights back, though Black still keeps a decisive advantage (-31.56 → -28.96, Stockfish:16). The line [pv:axb5 Kd6 b6 Bc5+ Kd3] wins the b-pawn and pushes b6, yet after...Kd6 Black is set to begin the king march, and Bc5+ forces the white king back to d3. Kd3 at the outset is a comparable option that also leaves Black with a decisive advantage [pv:Kd3 Kd6 c7 Rc5 c8=Q].

Black's 59...Kd6 maintains the advantage (-29.18, Stockfish:16), setting up the king march in [pv:Kd6 Kc4 Kc7 Kd4 Kb6] that White answers with Kc4 on the next turn. That is clearly stronger than the runner-up 59...Be1, which leaves Black with a decisive advantage but is clearly weaker once White pushes c7 in [pv:Be1 c7 Kd7 c8=Q+ Kxc8].

White's 60.Kc4 leaves Black with a decisive advantage (-29.18, Stockfish:16). The king march in [pv:Kc4 Kc7 Kd4 Kb6 Kd5] follows the same route as with Ke4, pressing toward d5, but neither entry square fixes White's plight—Kd5 itself would still leave Black with a decisive advantage. Ke4 is a comparable option that also leaves Black with a decisive advantage [pv:Ke4 Kc7 Kd4 Kb6 Kd5].

Kd5 is the most accurate move, yet it still leaves Black with a decisive advantage (-31.59, Stockfish:16). The continuation [pv:Kd5 Bb8 Ke6 Kxb5 Kd7] is White's best try in a difficult endgame. Kd4 is a roughly comparable option that also leaves Black with a decisive advantage, following [pv:Kd4 Kxb5 Ke4 Kxc6 Kd4], though Kd5 remains the stronger choice. Black went on to win.
